newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW - Strong team needed for Thai economy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Strong team needed for Thai economy.

text.p: Thailand's new government must form a competent team to tackle the country's high payments deficit, poor infrastructure and other economic problems, Kenneth Courtis, strategist and chief economist of Deutsche Bank Capital Markets, said.

"Thailand is at a crossroad. The recreation is over and now it is very important that (the government) has to get down to real economic management of the country," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Chavalit Yongchaiyuth, set to become Thailand's new prime minister, has yet to form a cabinet after his New Aspiration Party won the most parlimentary seats in the November 17 general election.

But he pledged during the pre-election campaign to include capable outsiders to key economic portfolios. Amnuay Viravan, a finance minister in 1980-1981, was tipped to be given a finance portfolio even though he did not run in the election.

One of the shortcomings many analysts said led to the downfall of Thai caretaker prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa was alleged corruption and mismanagement which eroded investors' confidence in the country.
Courtis said the slowdown in Thai economy was structural, cyclical and political.

"It is cyclical in a sense that the economy was overheated, the current account got too big. It is structural in the sense of new competition, of the need to accelerate infrastructure and the need to put more emphasis on quality education," he said.

"It is also political...it's the question of confidence. When these things go wrong at once, then you will have a crisis of confidence that you've had both among domestic and international investors," he added.

The Bank of Thailand forecast the gross domestic product (GDP) this year will grow 7.8 percent compared with 8.6 percent last year. The current account deficit is expected to reach 7.8 percent of GDP.

But some economists projected that the 1996 growth rate would be only slightly higher than six percent, its slowest rate in 10 years, as exports will probably rise only three to five percent this year against 23.6 percent growth in 1995.

"Investors' attitude at the moment is wait-and-see. Don't invest or commit a big amount of money until you see the course ahead...the people that will have key positions and see whether they will have the mandate to move ahead," he said.
However, Courtis forecast that 1997 growth rate would still be a moderate 6.5-7.0 percent.
Foreign investment in new industry such as automobiles, lower interest rates and inflation are seen as positive factors to will spur growth.
